title: Best Time to Visit Lumbini: Seasons and Heat
meta_description: When to visit Lumbini: month-by-month temperatures, winter fog, spring heat, the monsoon, Buddha Jayanti, and how to plan sightseeing around the heat.
summary: The best time to visit Lumbini is October to March, when days are dry and 20–30 °C. November and February are ideal. December and January bring cold, foggy mornings. From April to June the plains regularly pass 38 °C, and June to September is hot, humid and wet. Plan sightseeing for early morning and late afternoon.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: Lumbini lies on the Terai plains at about 110 m, a few kilometres from the Indian border, and its climate is closer to that of north India than to the Kathmandu Valley. Summers are long and very hot, the monsoon is humid and wet, and winters are mild by day and cool at night, with dense fog on many mornings.

For most travellers the best months are October, November, February and March. Days are warm and dry, skies are mostly clear and you can spend long hours outdoors. December and January are good too, especially for pilgrims, but mornings can be cold and grey, and fog sometimes delays flights. April to September is possible with planning, but heat or rain will shape every day.

sections.heading: Winter: December to February
paras: Winter is pilgrim season. Groups from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Vietnam and India arrive in large numbers, and the Sacred Garden is full of chanting. Daytime temperatures are pleasant, around 20–25 °C by afternoon, but nights drop to 7–10 °C, which feels colder in unheated rooms.

The defining feature of winter on the Terai is fog. On many mornings in late December and January, a thick, cold fog settles over the plains and may not lift until late morning, sometimes not at all for days. Locals call these spells sheetlahar, cold waves, and they hit poorer households hard. For visitors, fog means grey light, cold dawns in the garden and the risk of delayed morning flights at Bhairahawa. Bring a warm jacket, a hat and a scarf, and leave some slack in your plans.

By February the fog thins, the days lengthen and the mustard fields around Lumbini turn yellow. It is one of the loveliest months to visit. Wheat and lentils grow green in the fields, and the sarus cranes are easy to spot in the open farmland.

sections.heading: Spring and the hot season: March to May
paras: March is warm and still very pleasant, with afternoons around 30 °C. From April the heat builds quickly. By May, afternoon temperatures commonly reach 38–40 °C and sometimes more, and a hot, dry westerly wind, the loo, blows across the plains in the afternoon. Brick paths and stone floors become too hot to walk on barefoot by midday.

Spring is also harvest time. In March and April the wheat in the fields around Lumbini turns gold, and families cut and thresh it by hand and by machine along the roadsides. Mornings in early spring are among the most beautiful of the year, with soft light over the fields and the first heat not yet arrived.

This is also the season of Buddha Jayanti, the Buddha's birthday, on the full moon of Baisakh, usually in late April or May. It is the most important day of the year in Lumbini, with ceremonies, processions and huge crowds. If you come for it, accept the heat as part of the pilgrimage and plan everything for dawn and dusk.

sections.heading: Monsoon: June to September
paras: The monsoon usually arrives in mid-June and lasts until late September, bringing most of the year's rain. Afternoons are hot and very humid, around 32–35 °C, with heavy downpours that can last hours. Paths in the monastic zone flood in places, rural roads to Tilaurakot and Ramagrama turn muddy, and mosquitoes are active.

The monsoon is also the busiest time in the fields. Rice is transplanted from late June into July, and on the national paddy day, 15 Asar in the Nepali calendar, usually around the end of June, farming families plant together in the mud, singing and throwing it at each other. Cycling past the paddies on a dry morning is one of the season's quiet pleasures.

There are rewards. The rice fields are bright green, the Sacred Garden is quiet and the light after rain is clear. Hotels offer lower rates. If you visit now, use insect repellent, carry an umbrella, and keep a flexible plan for days when the rain does not stop.

sections.heading: Autumn: October and November
paras: When the monsoon ends, the air clears, the heat eases and Lumbini is at its best. October is still warm, with afternoons around 30 °C; November is cooler and drier. Both months are ideal for cycling the monastic zone and for day trips to the Kapilavastu sites.

Autumn is also Nepal's main festival season. Dashain and Tihar, usually in October or November, mean many Nepalis travel home, so domestic flights and buses fill up and some businesses close for a few days. Chhath, celebrated soon after Tihar by communities on the plains, brings worshippers to ponds and rivers at sunrise and sunset to honour the sun. Check current dates before you travel and book flights early.

sections.heading: Adding Tansen, Pokhara or Chitwan
paras: Most visitors combine Lumbini with other parts of Nepal, and the seasons do not line up perfectly. Tansen, at about 1,350 m, is far cooler than Lumbini and stays pleasant from October to April, though winter mornings are cold. Pokhara's mountain views are clearest from October to early December and good until March; spring haze softens them from April. Chitwan's wildlife viewing is best from February to April, when the tall grass has been cut and animals come to the rivers, but it shares Lumbini's heat from April.

Taken together, the window from October to March works well for a route that joins Lumbini with the hills and the jungle. If you can only travel in spring, start in Lumbini in March before the worst heat, then move up to Tansen and Pokhara as the plains warm up.

sections.heading: Coping with the heat
paras: Heat is the main health risk for visitors to Lumbini from April to September. Plan the day the way local people do: out early, indoors at midday, out again late. Drink more water than you think you need, add oral rehydration salts on hot days, and watch for headache, dizziness or nausea, which are early signs of heat exhaustion. Rest in shade and cool down at once if they appear.

Good hotels in Lumbini have air conditioning and backup power, and most also have generators or inverters for the occasional cut. Simpler guesthouses may only have fans. If you are visiting between April and September, we book rooms with reliable cooling and ask for rooms away from the afternoon sun.

Wear loose, light-coloured cotton, a wide hat and sunglasses

faqs.q: What is the best month to visit Lumbini?
faqs.a: November and February are the best months for most travellers: dry, sunny and comfortable, with afternoons around 25–28 °C and cool nights. October and March are almost as good, though a little warmer. December and January suit pilgrims well but bring cold, foggy mornings. Avoid May to August unless you have a special reason.

Very hot. From April to June, afternoon temperatures commonly reach 38–40 °C and occasionally more, with a hot dry wind called the loo. During the monsoon, temperatures drop slightly but humidity makes it feel just as hot. Plan sightseeing for early morning and late afternoon, and rest indoors in between.

faqs.q: Is there fog in Lumbini in winter?
faqs.a: Yes. In late December and January thick fog often covers the Terai plains in the morning and can last until late morning or, during cold waves, for several days. It makes dawns cold and grey and can delay flights at Bhairahawa. By February it usually clears. Bring warm layers and keep your schedule flexible.

faqs.q: When is Buddha Jayanti in Lumbini?
faqs.a: Buddha Jayanti, the Buddha's birthday, falls on the full moon of the Nepali month of Baisakh, usually in late April or May. The date changes each year with the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel. Lumbini holds ceremonies and processions, and the Sacred Garden is very crowded and hot.

faqs.q: Can I visit Lumbini during the monsoon?
faqs.a: Yes. The Sacred Garden and monasteries stay open, and the landscape is green and quiet. Expect heavy rain, high humidity, some flooded paths and muddy rural roads to Tilaurakot and Ramagrama. Flights can be delayed. Use mosquito repellent, carry an umbrella and plan indoor time for the heaviest rain.

faqs.q: What should I pack for Lumbini?
faqs.a: From March to October: loose, light cotton covering shoulders and knees, a wide hat, sunglasses, sunscreen, a refillable bottle, rehydration salts and mosquito repellent. From December to February add a warm jacket, scarf and hat for cold, foggy mornings. All year bring slip-on shoes and socks for temple visits.

Winter is the main pilgrimage season, so the Sacred Garden and some monasteries are busy with large groups, especially in the middle of the day. Early mornings and late afternoons are calmer. Hotels fill on festival dates and around Buddhist holidays in Asia, so book ahead from November to February.

faqs.q: How does Lumbini's weather compare with Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Lumbini is much hotter. At about 110 m, compared with about 1,400 m in Kathmandu, it is typically 5–10 °C warmer in winter and can be 10 °C or more warmer in the hot season. Kathmandu winters have frosty nights; Lumbini has fog instead. Pack for both if you are visiting each.

faqs.q: Is it worth visiting Lumbini in summer?
faqs.a: It can be, if summer is your only chance. Start at dawn, finish outdoor visits by late morning, rest through the afternoon in an air-conditioned room and go out again after 4 pm. You will have quieter sites and lower hotel rates. Travellers sensitive to heat, young children and older visitors should choose another season.
